headline_marked: [[Ukraine's kamikaze drones get US AI]] to track targets autonomously
headline: Ukraine's kamikaze drones get US AI to track targets autonomously
summary: A $100 million deal equips 50,000 Ukrainian Shrike drones with US-developed AI, enabling them to autonomously home in on moving targets even if they lose radio signal or GPS.
details: A $100 million deal will equip 50,000 Ukrainian Shrike drones with US-developed AI capabilities. The Shrike drones, made by SkyFall, will integrate Auterion's Skynode S strike kits, allowing them to autonomously track and strike moving targets. Deliveries began in mid-July.

Operators can manually fly the first-person view (FPV) drones into a battlefield area, designate a target up to half a mile away, and then activate a "fire-and-forget" terminal guidance mode. This allows the drone to proceed to the target without further human input.

The system enables autonomous tracking and striking even if the drone loses its connection with the operator due to signal blocking or enemy jamming. Auterion's software uses only visual information from the onboard camera, making it independent of GPS, a critical advantage against common GPS jamming.

This upgrade is expected to enhance the success rate of Shrike drones, which have already destroyed numerous Russian armored vehicles and even helicopters. While Ukraine has used other AI-powered drones for long-range strikes, this focuses on cheaper, shorter-range FPV drones for frontline combat.

Each AI-equipped Shrike drone costs about $2,000, compared to $400 for a manually piloted version. This is significantly more cost-effective than Western precision munitions, which can cost six or seven figures per shot.

The initial 50,000-drone order is funded by an unnamed European country, reportedly Germany. Auterion also has a $50 million Pentagon contract to deliver 33,000 more strike kits by July 2025, with future software updates potentially enabling autonomous drone swarms.

headline_marked: [[Apple caps security bug reports]] amid surge in AI-generated findings
headline: Apple caps security bug reports amid surge in AI-generated findings
summary: Apple has adjusted its bug bounty program, setting limits on submissions due to a significant increase in low-quality, AI-generated security reports.
details: Apple has recently implemented changes to its bug bounty program. These adjustments come as the company faces a substantial influx of what it describes as "AI slop" security reports.
The surge in AI-generated findings has led to a reduction in the overall quality of submissions, making it harder for Apple's security teams to identify legitimate and critical vulnerabilities.

By capping the number of reports, Apple aims to streamline the process and encourage researchers to submit higher-quality, thoroughly vetted bug reports. This move is intended to ensure the program remains effective in enhancing product security.
